title: The forgiven
hook: Hind, Ikrimah, Wahshi and others who fought him are forgiven when they come to him

segments.voice: Yesterday, sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house, and safety for anyone behind a closed door. Your line was: whoever shuts his door is safe. Who did you help feel safe? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

This week walked a long road. A pledge under a tree. A title rubbed out for peace. A wife's advice: do it first. An emperor's questions. A flag at Khaybar. A city of closed doors. And now, with Mecca entered, a harder question. What happens to the people who had hurt him badly? A man who killed the Prophet's uncle. A woman who celebrated that death. The son of a leading opponent. One by one, they come. Today: the forgiven.
screen: `A WEEK ON THE ROAD.` → `MECCA ENTERED.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE ONES WHO HURT HIM?`

segments.voice: Start with Wahshi. At Uhud he killed Hamza, the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps Wahshi's own account. Later, he comes to the Prophet with a group from Ta'if, and accepts Islam. The Prophet asks: are you Wahshi? Are you the one who killed Hamza? Wahshi says it happened as he's heard. And the Prophet accepts him, and then asks one thing: can you keep your face away from me? That detail is honest. Forgiveness here doesn't mean the grief is gone. The door is open, and the wound is still a wound. Then Hind, Abu Sufyan's wife, who had stood against him at Uhud. Bukhari records what she said to him after she accepted Islam: once there was no household on earth she wanted more to see disgraced than his, and now there's none she wants more to see honored. Then Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, who fled Mecca toward Yemen to escape. The sirah tells that his wife, Umm Hakim, asked the Prophet for his safety, got it, and went after her husband to bring him home. He was received, not punished. Notice what these stories have in common. None of the three earns it by being useful first. Each one simply comes. And each one is met by a door that was already open. That doesn't erase what they did. The stories remember it plainly, right beside Hind's sentence about a household she now wanted to see honored.
screen: `WAHSHI: KEEP YOUR FACE AWAY.` · `HIND: NOW, HONORED.` · `IKRIMAH: BROUGHT HOME BY HIS WIFE.` · `EACH ONE SIMPLY COMES.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYED OPEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: forgive a real hurt. Sit still for a moment, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one real hurt, not the biggest one, one you can hold for two minutes. Let yourself remember it plainly, the way the stories remember Uhud. Then notice: forgiving doesn't require pretending it didn't hurt. The Prophet still asked Wahshi to keep his face away. You can keep a boundary and still open a door. Picture leaving that door unlocked, even a crack. If you pray, you can ask Allah to forgive them, and to forgive you. The bell holds the time.
The forgiven. Wahshi, Hind, Ikrimah and others who had fought the Prophet were accepted when they came to him, their past remembered but not held against them. Today's word.
Your line: the door stayed open. Today, leave one door open a crack for someone who hurt you. A boundary can stay. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and the stories of Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah are told as examples of the Prophet's mercy toward former enemies.

myth: forgiving Wahshi meant the Prophet acted as if nothing happened
he accepted him, and asked him to keep his face away.
Ikrimah's wife asked for his safety and brought him back
the sirah tells Umm Hakim went after him once his safety was granted.
the forgiven had to prove themselves useful first
each one simply came, and was received.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. the man who killed your uncle stands in front of you and accepts Islam. what do you do?
options: accept him, and ask him to keep his face away from you.
accept him and say it never happened.
fork.reveal: he accepted Wahshi, and asked: can you keep your face away from me? the door was open, and the grief was honest.

original.note: Arabic: pardon, letting a wrong go; al-'Afuw, the Pardoner, is one of the names of Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone was forgiven, end of story.
what it means: forgiveness that remembers plainly, keeps an honest boundary, and still lets people come home.
what a scholar hears: Wahshi's own account of Hamza's death and his later acceptance of Islam, preserved in Bukhari's book of military campaigns.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 (Hind's words to the Prophet)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; Malik, al-Muwatta, book of marriage (Ikrimah and Umm Hakim)

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): checked Wahshi (Bukhari 4072), Hind (3825) and Ikrimah (Muwatta); fixed a garbled review note; no voice changes.

Editor: Wahshi now comes later with a group from Ta'if, as his account in Bukhari says; Ikrimah fled toward Yemen (Muwatta), not 'the coast'; stock ending ('refuse to let it be the last chapter') replaced with a concrete detail.
Hadith numbers (Bukhari 4072, 3825) and the Muwatta reference for Ikrimah given from memory; confirm.
Wahshi's acceptance of Islam came after the conquest (with a delegation from Ta'if, per his account), not on the day of the conquest; the script does not date it. Confirm framing.
'Fled toward the coast' for Ikrimah: sources mention Yemen and a sea crossing; confirm wording.
Hind 'stood against him at Uhud' and 'celebrated that death' follow the sirah; confirm.
'The son of a leading opponent' (Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl) is already softened; no superlative remains.
Al-'Afuw as a divine name in the original note; confirm.
